definition: The circuit, rim, or surrounding edge, of a thing;
sourceDefinition: The circuit, rim, or surrounding edge, of a thing; what surrounds [ the whole of] a thing: (S, K:) pl. HuturN . (S.) ― -b2- The hoop of a sieve [and the like]. (TA.) ― -b3- The anus; syn. Haloqapu Ald~uburi ; (K;) or such is the meaning HitaAru Ald~uburi , and $arajuhu : (Mgh in art. $rj :) and the extremities of its skin; i. e. the place where the external skin and the extremities of the xaworaAn [or rectum ] meet: or the edges of the dubur [or anus ]: (TA:) or the part between the anus and the anterior pudendum: or the line between the two testicles. (K.) ― -b4- HitaAru AlA^u*uni The circuit of the edges of the gristles of the ear. (TA.) ― -b5- HitaAru AlEayoni The edges of the eyelids, which meet when the eye is closed: (TA:) or the ziyq of the eyelid, (K accord. to some copies, [and this is the right reading, meaning its edge, zyq being here used tropically, its proper signification being the “ part ” of a shirt “ that surrounds the neck, ”] as is said in the TA,) internally: in most copies of the K rayoqu Aljafoni , [in the CK riyqu Aljufoni ,] with rA' [not zAY ]. (TA.) ― -b6- HitaAru AlZ~ufuri The part of the flesh which is around the nail. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) or ↓ HidaA^N , [but see what follows,] sometimes pronounced ↓ HadaA^N , (Mgh,) [The kite; vulgarly called HidaAyap ;] a certain bird, (S, Mgh, K,) well known; (S, K;) a certain noxious bird; (Msb;) surnamed A^abuwAlxaT~aAfi and Abw AlS~aloti ; (TA;) that preys upon large field-rats ( jiro*aAn ): (Mgh, TA:) J and Sgh say that the word should not be pronounced ↓ HadaA^apN ; but AHei mentions this pronunciation on the authority of [some of] the Arabs; and accord. to IAar and IAmb, the faA^os [see above] and this bird were sometimes called alike ↓ HadaA^apN and ↓ HadaA^N : the more approved pronunciation of the name of the bird, however, is with kesr [i. e. HidaA^apN ]: the pl. is ↓ HidaA^N (S, Msb, K) and HidaA='N , (K,) both extr., (TA,) [or rather the former is a coll. gen. n.,] and HidoA=nN : (Msb, K:) and the following are variations of the name of this bird: Hud~aY , and Huday~aA , (TA,) the latter said by AHát to be an erroneous form of the word, used by the people of El-Hijáz, (Mgh, TA,) and ↓ Hudayoy^iyapN , app. a dim., for ↓ Hudayoy^apN , also pronounced Huday~apN , (TS, TA,) and Huduw~N , occurring in a trad. in conjunction with A^ufoEuw~N [for A^afoEFY ], (Mgh, TA,) of the dial. of the people of Mekkeh. (TA in art. Hdw .) Hence the saying, waraA='aki bunoduqap ↓ HidaA^a HidaA^a , (S, K, TA,) for which the vulgar say, HadaA HadaA , (S,) [accord. to some, meaning O kite, O kite, a bullet is behind thee: accord. to others, O Ḥidà, O Ḥidà, Bunduḳah is behind thee: ] Esh-Sharḳee (Ibn-El-Ḳuṭámee, Ta) Says, (S,) HidaA^N and bunoduqapu were two tribes, descendants of HidaA^u bonu namirapa and bunoduqapu bonu maZ~apa , (S, K, *) and both of saEodu AlEa$iyrapi ; (S, TA;) the former in El-Koofeh, and the latter in El-Yemen: the former attacked the latter, and obtained spoil from them; and then the latter attacked the former, and destroyed them: (TA:) and hence this saying: (S, K, TA:) or HidaA^a is here an apocopated form of HidaA^ap : (S, K:) so says ISk: (S:) and AO says that by it is here meant the bird [i. e. the kite]; and by bndqp , the thing with which one shoots [from a cross-bow, namely, a bullet]; and the prov. is used to caution a person: accord. to Ibn-El-Kelbee, it is applied to him who esteems himself cunning in an affair, and is outwitted therein by another: accord. to the A, to him who is threatened with an evil near at hand. (TA.) -A2- HidaA^apN also signifies The saAlifap (meaning the fore part, TA, [or the fore part from beneath the ear to the middle of the collarbone, ]) of the neck of a horse: (As, K:) pl. HidaA='N . (As, TA.) -A3- See also HadaA^apN .

definition: A walled garden;
sourceDefinition: A walled garden; a garden surrounded by a wall: (S, Msb, TA:) of the measure faEiylapN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlapN : (Msb:) or any round piece of land surrounded by a fence or the like, or by elevated land: (TA:) or whatever is surrounded by building: (K:) and, by extension of its application, a garden, though without a wall: (Msb:) or a meadow, or garden, ( rawoDap ,) having trees: (S, K:) or a garden of palm-trees and of other trees, (Zj, IDrd, K,) dense and luxuriant, (Zj, IDrd, TA,) and, as some say, fruit-bearing: (TA:) or a garden ( jan~ap ) of palmtrees and grape-vines: (TA:) or a distinct collection of palm-trees: (K:) or a plot of seedproduce: (Kr, TA:) or a hollow in a valley, that retains water: and any depressed place in a valley, that retains water, thought water be not in its bottom: (TA:) pl. HadaAy^iqu . (S, Msb, K.) Hence the saying, wa rada EalaY~a kitaAbuka fatanaz~ahotu fiY bahojapi HadaAy^iqihi (tropical:) [ Thy letter has come to me, and I have recreated myself in contemplating the beauty of its garden-like phrases ]. sourceDefinition: , inf. n. A_iHoraAzN , He kept, preserved, or guarded, it; he took care of it; (TA;) as also ↓ Harazahu , (K,) aor. , (TK,) inf. n. HarozN ; (TA;) or the latter is formed by substitution of a letter from Harasahu : (K:) or the former signifies he put it in a Hiroz [q. v.]; (Mgh, Msb;) and so ↓ the latter: (TA:) and the former, he preserved it from being taken. (TA.) You say, A^aHorarahu fiY wiEaAy^ihi [ He kept, or preserved, it in his, or its, receptacle ]. (A.) And A^aHorazotu AlmataAEa I put the goods into the Hiroz . (Msb.) And A^anofasakumo ↓ Har~izuwA Preserve ye, or guard ye, yourselves: (A:) [or do so strenuously; for it is said that] Hr~zhu , inf. n. taHoriyzN , signifies he took extraordinary pains in keeping, preserving, or guarding, it. (K.) You say also A^aHorazato farojahaA She (a woman, TA) guarded her pudendum; (K, TA;) as though she put it in an inaccessible Hiroz . (TA.) And AHrz AlmakaAnu Alr~ajula The place protected the man; afforded him refuge; as also ↓ Hr~zhu , (K,) inf. n. taHoriyzN . (TA.) ― -b2- He made it firm, or strong. (KL.) [ He fortified it, or protected it against attack: see Haruza .] ― -b3- He drew, collected, or gathered, it together; (Msb, TA;) as also ↓ Harazahu , [aor. ,] inf. n. HarozN . (TA.) Hence, (Msb,) A^aHoraza qaSaba Als~aboqi He grasped, or clutched, the winning-canes; he got them for himself: (Msb:) (tropical:) he outstripped; outran; or won the race. (A, TA. See qaSabN .) [Hence also,] A^aHoraza AlA^ajora He took, received, or got possession of, the recompense, reward, hire, pay, or wages; syn. HaAzahu . (K.) Whence the prov., A^aHorazotu nahobiY wa A^abotagiY Aln~awaAfila [ I have gained my spoil, and I seek the superabundant gain ]: originally said by Aboo-Bekr: he used to perform the prayer called Alwtr in the beginning of the night, and to say these words; meaning, that he had performed his witor , and was safe from its escaping his observance, and that he had gained his recompense for it; and if he awoke in the night, would perform the supererogatory prayers. (TA.) You say also, A^aHoraza AlxaTara [ He won the bet ]. (A in art. xTr .)

definition: [is applied, app.
sourceDefinition: [is applied, app. in the classical language, as it is in the present day, to Various species of thistle, and other prickly plants: also to the heads of thistles and the like: and particularly to the caltrop, or tribulus: and hence the explanations here following:] the Hasak [or prickly heads ] of the [plant called] saEodaAn : (S:) or a certain herb, (Aboo-Ziyád, Mgh, TA,) inclining to yellowness, (Aboo-Ziyád, TA,) having [a head of] prickles of rounded form: (Aboo-Ziyád, Mgh, TA:) seldom, or never, does any one walk upon it, when it has dried up, without putting upon his feet boots or sandals: and the ants transport its produce [or heads ] to their nests: (Aboo-Ziyád, TA:) a certain plant, the produce [or head ] whereof (which is rough [or prickly ], TA) clings to the wool of sheep, (K,) and to the fur of camels, in their places of pasturing: (TA:) its leaves are like those of purslane ( Alr~ijolap ), or narrower, and at its leaves are compact and hard prickles, having three forks: [hence it seems to be a species of three-horned caltrop: or for “ three, ” we should perhaps read four: (see another application of the word in what follows:)] the drinking [of an infusion] thereof has the effect of crumbling the stone of the kidneys and bladder; and the drinking of the expressed juice of its leaves is good for the venereal faculty, and for difficulty in the discharge of urine, and for the bite of vipers; and the sprinkling it in the dwelling kills fleas: (K:) also, accord. to Aboo-Nasr, the produce of the [plant called] nafal : (TA:) and sharp. hard prickles or thorns: (TA in art. msk :) n. un. with p : (S, Mgh:) which some hold to apply to any fruit, or produce, of a plant, that is of the kind termed EuqodapN [i. e. forming a compact and roundish head ]; and hence, to the pod of the cotton-plant: and it also signifies a prickle, or thorn. (TA.) [Hence,] ↓ A_in~ahu laHasakapN (tropical:) Verily he is rough. (A, TA.) And A_in~ahumo laHasakN A^amoraAsN (assumed tropical:) Verily they are strong: and of one person you say marisN ↓ HasakapN . (TA.) And masakapN ↓ huwa HasakapN (tropical:) He is courageous: (K and TA in art. msk :) and of a number of persons you say HasakN masakN . (TA in that art., q. v.) [See also HasikN .] ― -b2- See also HasiykapN ― -b3- Also [(assumed tropical:) Caltrops, as meaning] a kind of instrument used in war, (S, K,) made like the Hasak mentioned in the first sentence of this paragraph, (S,) or like the prickles of the Hasak , (K,) of iron, (S, K,) or of canes, (K,) and sometimes of wood, (TA,) and cast, (K,) or set up, (TA,) around the army, (K, TA,) in the ways of the horses. (TA.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) Rancour, malevolence, malice, or spite; and enmity; (K, TA;) as also ↓ HasakapN , (K,) and ↓ HasiykapN and ↓ HusaAkapN . (S, K. [The last in the CK written HasAkap ; but expressly said in the TA to be with damm, and so written in copies of the S and K.]) You say, ↓ fiY Sadorihi EalaY~a HasiykapN and ↓ HusaAkapN [ In his bosom is rancour, &c., against me ]. (S.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. and , (S, Msb, K,) the former of which aors. is found in the seven readings of the Kur, (Msb,) inf. n. Ha$orN , (S, Msb, K,) He congregated, or collected together, (S, Msb, K,) men: (S, Msb:) or he congregated them, or collected them together, and drove them: (Msb, TA:) he made them to go forth, collected together, from one place to another: (Bd in lix. 2:) he, or it, compelled them to emigrate: (K, * TA: [in the CK AlxalaA='u is put by mistake for AljalaA'u , the explanation of the inf. n.:]) and [simply] he drove towards a place or quarter. (TA.) Hence yawomu AlHa$ori (tropical:) [ The day of congregation, &c.; meaning] the day of resurrection: (S, * TA:) [see also maHo$irN :] and suwrapu AlHa$ori (tropical:) [ The Chapter of the Compulsion to emigration; which is the fifty-ninth chapter of the Kur-an]. (TA.) It is said by most of the expositors of the Kur that the wild animals and other beasts, and even the flies, will be collected together ( tuHo$aru ) for retaliation; and they cite a trad. on this subject. (TA.) So in the Kur [lxxxi. 5], wa A_i*aA AlwuHuw$u Hu$irato And when the wild animals shall be collected together, (Bd, Jel,) from every quarter, (Bd,) after resurrection; (Jel;) or raised to life, (Bd,) for the purpose of their retaliating, one upon another; after which they shall return to dust: (Bd, Jel:) or the meaning is, shall die, (Az, S,) in the present world; accord. to some: (Az:) and thus says 'Ikrimeh, (S, TA,) on the authority of I'Ab, (TA,) as is related by Sa'eed Ibn-Masrook: (S, TA:) but accord. to some, the two meanings are nearly the same; for each denotes collection. (TA.) Ha$orN also signifies The going forth with a people fleeing or hastening or dispersing themselves in war; when used absolutely. (TA.) ― -b2- Ha$aratohumu Als~anapu , aor. and (Lth,) inf. n. Ha$orN , (K,) (tropical:) The year of dearth destroyed their camels and other quadrupeds; because it causes the owners to collect themselves from the various quarters to the cities or towns: (Lth:) or it caused them to go down to the cities or towns: (A:) or it distressed them; app., because of their collecting themselves together from the desert to the places of settled abodes: (Abu-t- Teiyib:) and Ha$arati Als~anapu maAla fulaAnK The year of dearth destroyed the camels &c. of such a one. (S, K. *) -A2- Ha$arahu , (S, A,) inf. n. Ha$orN , (S, K,) (tropical:) He made it (a spear-head, S, A) thin, or slender: (S, A, K:) he made it (a spear-head, and a knife,) sharp, or pointed, and thin, or slender: (TA:) he made it small, and thin, or slender: (Th:) he pared it; namely, a stick: (TA:) he pared it, and made it sharp, or pointed. (S.)

(TA.)

definition: The first of grapes, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) such as are crude and sour, (Msb,) or as long as they remain green: (K:) or grapes when hard: (Az, TA:) or, accord.
sourceDefinition: The first of grapes, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) such as are crude and sour, (Msb,) or as long as they remain green: (K:) or grapes when hard: (Az, TA:) or, accord. to AHn, grapes when they have become organized and compacted: or, as he says on one occasion, [the n. un.] HiSorimapN signifies a grape when it germinates. (TA.) The rubbing of the body in the bath with bruised, or pulverized, HSrm dried in the shade prevents the origination of [the cutaneous disorder termed] HaSaf in the year in which this is done, and strengthens the body, and cools it. (K.) ― -b2- Dates, or fruit, ( tamorN , or vamarN , accord. to different copies of the K, the latter being the reading in the M, TA,) not yet ripe. (M, K, TA.) ― -b3- Fruit plucked from the tree called the maZ~ , (K,) i. e. the wild pomegranate. (TA.) ― -b4- In the “ Jema et-Tefáreek, ” it is said to signify Grape-stones: but this requires consideration. (Mgh.) ― -b5- What is lean, dry, or withered, (syn. Ha$afN ,) of anything. (AZ, Msb, K.) ― -b6- And hence, (Msb,) (assumed tropical:) A niggardly man; (ISk, S, Msb, K;) arrow in disposition; as also ↓ muHaSoramN (S, TA) and ↓ mutaHaSorimN : (K, * TA:) or ↓ muHaSoramN means having little, or no, good. (TA.) ― -b7- Short; (K;) and faAHi$ [app. as meaning evil in disposition ]; as also ↓ HuSorumN . (TA.) ― -b8- And An iron [ hooked ] instrument with which the bucket is extracted from a well; (K;) also called EawodaqN . (TA.)

HaTamN , It broke, or became broken, in pieces; as also ↓ AnHTm (Msb) and ↓ tHT~m : (TA:) or these two, (S, K,) or [correctly] the former [only], (TA,) it broke, or became broken: (S, K, TA:) or they are peculiarly said of that which is dry, or tough; (K, TA;) as a bone and the like. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] HaTimati Ald~aAb~apu (assumed tropical:) The beast became aged [ and emaciated and weak, or broken with age: see HaTimN , below]. (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- He, or it, crushed it, or bruised it; as, for instance, a lion, that which he devours; and as a camel and a sheep or goat, the ground with his feet or hoofs, and the trees and herbs in eating them; and as the wind, that upon which it blows [vehemently]. (A, TA.) ― -b3- One says also, laA taHoTimo EalayonaA AlmarotaEa , meaning (tropical:) Spoil not thou to us the pasturage by pasturing upon it. (TA.) ― -b4- And HaTama fulaAnFA A^aholuhu (tropical:) His family rendered such a one a broken old man; as though they loaded him with their burdens. (TA.) And HaTamatohu Als~in~u (S) (assumed tropical:) Age rendered him infirm. (TA.)

definition: A vehement fire, (K,) that breaks in pieces everything that is cast into it.
sourceDefinition: A vehement fire, (K,) that breaks in pieces everything that is cast into it. (TA.) Hence, (S, TA,) AlHuTamapu a name of Hell, (K,) or of Hell-fire: (S, K:) or, as some say, the fourth stage of Hell: (Har. p. 347:) or a gate of Hell. (K.) ― -b2- (tropical:) A man who eats much; (S, TA;) as also ↓ HuTamN ; who breaks everything in eating: (Har p. 580:) and the latter, and ↓ HuTumN , an insatiable man. (TA.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) A large number of camels, (T, S, K,) and of sheep or goats: (T, K:) because they break, or crush, (T, S, TA,) the herbage, (T, TA,) or everything, (S, TA,) or the ground with their feet or hoofs, and the trees and herbs in eating them. (TA.) ― -b4- Also, and ↓ HuTamN , (S, K,) (tropical:) A pastor having little mercy upon the cattle; (S, TA;) or who acts injuriously towards them; (K, TA;) causing them to crush, or bruise, one another; (S, K, TA;) or as though he crushed, or bruised, them by his vehement driving: (A, TA:) or the former signifies a pastor who does not allow his beasts to avail themselves of the plentiful pasturages, nor let them disperse themselves in the pasturage: and ↓ the latter, one who is ungentle, or rough; as though he broke, or crushed, or bruised, them when driving them or pasturing them: and ↓ saw~aAqN HuTamN signifies a man who drives beasts vehemently, crushing them, or bruising them, by reason of his vehement driving; but it is used by way of comparison, as meaning (tropical:) cunning and versatile. (TA.) Hence, $ar~u Alr~iEaA='i AlHuTamapu [ The worst of pastors is the ungentle, who causes the beasts to crush, or bruise, one another ]: (S, K:) accord. to the S, a prov.: accord. to Sgh and the K, not a prov., but a trad.: but many of the trads. are reckoned among provs.: it is applied to him who governs, or manages, ill. (MF, TA.) Hence also what is related in a trad. of 'Alee, that Kureysh, when they saw him in war, or battle, used to say, AiHo*aruwA AlHuTama ↓ AiHo*aruwA AlHuTama [ Beware ye of the rough one! Beware ye of the rough one! ]. (TA.)

Hence, yaA EaAqidu A@*okuro Hal~FA [ O tyer of a knot, bear in mind the time of untying: or HaAbilu O binder, or tyer, of the rope: (see art. Hbl :)] (S, TA:) or, as IAar relates it, yA HaAmilu [ O loader ]: a prov., applied to the consideration of results; because a man may tie a load too tightly; and when he desires to untie it, may injure himself and his camel. (TA. [See also a similar saying below, in the second paragraph.]) And Al$~ufoEapu kaHal~i AlEiqaAli [ The right of preemption is like the untying of the cord with which a camel's fore shank and arm are bound together ]: meaning that it is accomplished as quickly and easily as the EqAl is untied: the explanation that it passes away quickly, like the camel when his EqAl is untied, is improbable. (Mgh, Msb. *) And hence the saying [in the Kur xx. 28], wa A@Holulo EuqodapF mino lisaAniY (assumed tropical:) [ And loose Thou an impediment of, or from, my tongue ]. (Er-Rághib, TA.) The pass. is pronounced by some Hul~a , and by others Hil~a : thus in the saying of El-Farezdak, famaA Hil~a mino jaholK HubaY HulamaAy^inaA wa laA qaAbilu AlmaEoruwfi fiynaA yuEan~afu [ And the garments of our forbearing men by which they support themselves in sitting by binding them, or making them tight, round the shanks and back are not loosed through ignorance, nor is the accepter of the benefit, among us, reproached ]; the kesreh of the first l [in the original form Hulila ] being transferred to the H : but Akh heard it pronounced in this instance Hul~a ; and some, he says, in this word, and in others like it, as rud~a and $ud~a , only impart to the dammeh somewhat of the sound of kesreh, by the pronunciation termed A_i$omaAm . (S, Msb, K) and , (K,) both of which forms of the aor. are mentioned by Ibn-Málik, (TA,) inf. n. HuluwlN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and Hal~N (S, K) and HalalN , which is extr., (K,) and maHal~N (S, TA) and maHil~N ; (TA;) and bihi ↓ AHtl~ (S, * K) and ↓ AHtl~hu ; (K;) meaning nazala bihi [ He alighted, or descended and stopped &c. HuluwlN , (S Msb,) (assumed tropical:) The debt was, or became, or fell, due; (K, * TA;) its appointed term, or period, ended, (Msb, TA,) so that the payment of it became due. (TA.) sourceDefinition: : see 1, in two places: ― -b2- and see also 4, in four places. ― -b3- Hl~l Alyamiyna , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. taHuliylN (Mgh, K) and ↓ taHil~apN , (S, * Mgh, K,) and ↓ taHil~N , which is anomalous, (K,) or ↓ taHil~apN is a simple subst., (Msb,) [and] so is ↓ Hil~N , (K, TA,) (assumed tropical:) He expiated the oath: (K:) or (assumed tropical:) he freed the oath from obligation by making an exception, or saying A_ino $aA='a A@ll~`hu , or by expiation: (Mgh, Msb:) or (assumed tropical:) he did that whereby he became free from violating, or failing of keeping, the oath; [generally meaning he made an exception in the oath, or he expiated it; ] as also ↓ Hal~ahaA : (Msb:) and fiY yamynh ↓ tHl~l (assumed tropical:) he made an exception, or said A_ino $aA='a A@ll~`hu , in his oath, (S, Mgh, K,) immediately: (TA:) and minohaA ↓ tHl~l (assumed tropical:) he became quit of it by expiation, (Mgh, TA,) or by a violation of it requiring expiation, or by making an exception, or saying An $A' All~`h , in it. (TA.) One says to him who goes to a great length in threatening, or him who exceeds the due bounds in what he says, A^abaA fulaAnK ↓ Hil~FA , meaning (assumed tropical:) Make thou an exception, or say An $A' All~`h , O father of such a one, in thine oath; regarding him as a swearer: and in like manner one says, ↓ yaA HaAlifu A@*okuro Hil~FA (assumed tropical:) [ O swearer, bear in mind the making an exception, or saying An $A' All~`h ]. (S, * TA. [See a similar saying in the second sentence of this art.]) In the saying laA^afoEalan~a ka*aA *`lika A^ano A^afoEala ka*aA ↓ A_il~aA Hil~a , [the particle] Al~A is syn. with l`kin~a ; and the meaning is said to be, (assumed tropical:) [ I will assuredly do such a thing: but ] the annulling of the obligation, or the expiation, of [ that ] my asseveration ( qasamiY ↓ taHil~apa , or taHoliylahu ,) shall be my doing such a thing. (TA.) One says also, Alqasami ↓ faEalotuhu taHil~apa , meaning (assumed tropical:) I did it only enough to annul the obligation of, or to expiate, the oath; not exceeding therein the ordinary bounds. (S, Msb.) It is said in a trad., laA yamuwtu Alqasami ↓ lilomuw^omini valaAvapu A^awolaAdK fatamas~ahu Aln~aAru A_il~aA taHil~apa , meaning (assumed tropical:) [ Three children of the believer shall not die and the fire of Hell touch him ]. save enough to annul the obligation of, or to expiate, the oath that is implied in the saying in the Kur [xix. 72], “ There is not any of you that shall not come to it. ” (A' Obeyd, S, TA.) Hence taHoliylN came to be applied to anything in which the ordinary bounds were not exceeded. (S, Msb.) One says, Darabotuhu taHoliylFA , (S, TA,) or DarobFA taHoliylFA , (K,) meaning (assumed tropical:) I beat him moderately; not exceeding the ordinary bounds. (K, * TA.) And Kaab Ibn-Zuheyr says, speaking of the feet of a she-camel, waqoEuhun~a AlA^aroDa taHoliylu , meaning Their falling on the ground is without vehemence. (S.) [In like manner, also,] Alqasami ↓ taHil~apa is descriptive, by way of comparison, of littleness; as is Alyamiyni ↓ taHil~apa : (Mgh:) or of anything occupying little time: (TA:) and Alqasami ↓ A_il~aA taHil~apa , in the trad. cited above, means (assumed tropical:) [ slightly, or] with a slight touch. (Mgh.) A poet says, A^araY A_ibiliY jaduwda falamo ta*uqo muqosami ↓ bihaA qaTorapF A_il~aA taHil~apa (assumed tropical:) [ I see my camels loathed the water of Jadood, so that they did not taste in it a drop save sparingly ]. (S.) ― -b4- Hl~l maA bihi mina Ald~aA='i , inf. n. taHoliylN , (assumed tropical:) He, or it, removed what was in him, of disease. (Har p. 231.) -A2- Hll~`hu AlHul~apa He clad him with the Hul~ap . (TA.)

One says to him who goes to a great length in threatening, or him who exceeds the due bounds in what he says, A^abaA fulaAnK ↓ Hil~FA , meaning (assumed tropical:) Make thou an exception, or say An $A' All~`h , O father of such a one, in thine oath; regarding him as a swearer: and in like manner one says, ↓ yaA HaAlifu A@*okuro Hil~FA (assumed tropical:) [ O swearer, bear in mind the making an exception, or saying An $A' All~`h ]. Hence taHoliylN came to be applied to anything in which the ordinary bounds were not exceeded. (S, Msb.) One says, Darabotuhu taHoliylFA , (S, TA,) or DarobFA taHoliylFA , (K,) meaning (assumed tropical:) I beat him moderately; not exceeding the ordinary bounds. (K, * TA.) And Kaab Ibn-Zuheyr says, speaking of the feet of a she-camel, waqoEuhun~a AlA^aroDa taHoliylu , meaning Their falling on the ground is without vehemence. (S.) definition: He alighted, or descended and stopped or sojourned or abode or lodged or settled, with him;
sourceDefinition: He alighted, or descended and stopped or sojourned or abode or lodged or settled, with him; and simply he took up his abode, lodged, or settled, with him; syn. Hal~a maEahu . (K.) You say, yuHaAl~uhu fiY daArK waAHidapK [ He takes up his abode, lodges, or settles, with him in one house ]. (S.) And, of a woman, tuHaAl~u zawojahaA fiY firaA$K [ She takes her place with her husband in a bed ]. (Mgh.) 4. AHl~hu He made him to alight, or descend and stop or sojourn or abide or lodge or settle; and simply he made him to take up his abode, to lodge, or to settle; syn. A^anozalahu ; (S, K;) as also ↓ Hll~`hu , and bihi ↓ Hal~a : (K:) said also of a place [as though meaning it invited him to alight, &c.]. (ISd, TA.) So in the phrases AHl~hu AlmakaAna and biAlomakaAni , and AlmakaAna ↓ Hll~`hu , He made him to alight, or descend and stop &c., in the place. (K.) ― -b2- AHl~ binafosihi (assumed tropical:) [ He caused punishment ( AlEuquwbapa being understood) to alight, or descend, upon himself; or] he did what necessitated, or he deserved, punishment. (S, K.) ― -b3- AHl~hu A@ll~`hu Ealayohi (assumed tropical:) God necessitated it, as suitable to the requirements of justice, to take effect upon him; namely, his threatened punishment ( A^amorahu ). (K, * TA.) ― -b4- And AHl~hu (tropical:) He (God, Msb and K, and a man, S, Msb) made it lawful, allowable, or free; as also ↓ Hll~`hu , (S, Mgh, Msb, K, TA,) inf. n. taHoliylN and ↓ taHil~apN . (S.) Hence, [in the Kur ii. 276,] A^aHal~a A@ll~`hu AlbayoEa (assumed tropical:) God has made selling to be lawful, or allowable, giving the choice to practise it or abstain from it. (Msb.) And hence also, A^aHolalotu lahu Al$~aYo'a (assumed tropical:) I made, or have made, lawful, allowable, or free, to him, the thing. (S.) And A^aHolalotu AlmaroA^apa lizawojihaA (assumed tropical:) I made, or have made, the woman lawful to her husband. (S.) ― -b5- And A^aHolalotuhu and ↓ Hal~alotuhu (assumed tropical:) I made him, or pronounced him, free from, or quit of, obligation, or responsibility, with respect to what was between me and him. Also (assumed tropical:) He entered upon [ any of ] the profane months. (S, K.) And (assumed tropical:) He went forth to the Hil~ : (S, K:) or he became in the Hil~ ; which means the region without the Haram [or sacred territory ]: (Msb:) or he became free from, or quit of, an obligation [ of any kind ] that was upon him. (S, K.) ― -b2- It is said in a trad., A^aHil~a bimano A^aHal~a bika , meaning (assumed tropical:) Whoso quits the state of A_iHoraAm , and makes it lawful to attack thee, and fights with thee, do thou so with him, though thou be in the state of AHrAm : or it means, if a man make lawful to him what is unlawful to him, as thy honour or reputation, and thy property, repel him from thyself in such a way as thou canst. (Sgh, TA.) ― -b3- AHl~t (assumed tropical:) She (a ewe or goat) secreted milk in her udder without bringing forth: (S, O:) or (assumed tropical:) she, (a ewe or goat, K, and a camel, TA,) after her milk had become scanty, or had dried up, yielded her milk abundantly in consequence of her having eaten the [ herbage termed ] rabiyE : in which case she is said to be ↓ muHil~N . (K.) And AHl~t EalaY waladihaA (assumed tropical:) She (a camel) yielded her milk abundantly to her young one. (ISd, TA.)

definition: [ A dress consisting of ] an A_izaAr [i.
sourceDefinition: [ A dress consisting of ] an A_izaAr [i. e. a waist-wrapper ] and a ridaA=' [or wrapper for the whole body ], (S, M, Mgh, K,) or a burod [which is another kind of wrapper for the whole body ], or some other garment: (M, K:) only applied to a dress consisting of two garments (S, M, Nh, Msb, K) of one kind: (Nh, Msb:) or either of the two garments by itself: or a ridaA=' and a shirt, completed by a turban; or a good garment; but not so called when upon a man; for in this case it means two garments, or three: or any good new garment that is worn, thick or coarse, or fine or thin: (TA:) or a lined garment: (K:) but with the Arabs of the desert it means [ a dress consisting of ] three garments, i. e. a shirt and an A_izaAr and a ridaA=' : (TA:) pl. HulalN (Msb) [and HilaAlN , as below]: accord. to A'Obeyd, HulalN means buruwd of El-Yemen, (S, TA,) from various places; and a garment of this kind is asserted to be meant in a trad. in which it is said that the best kind of grave-clothing is the Hul~ap : it is also said that HulalN is applied to the wa$oY and Hibar and xaz~ and qaz~ and quwhiY~ and marowiY~ and Hariyr . (TA.) ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) A weapon, or weapons: (Sgh, K:) pl. HulalN and HilaAlN . (K.) You say, labisa Hul~atahu , meaning (assumed tropical:) He wore, or put on, his weapon, or weapons. (Sgh, TA.) ― -b3- Also [like A_izaArN ] (tropical:) A wife. (TA.)

definition: (tropical:) Lawful, allowable, or free;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) Lawful, allowable, or free; contr. of HaraAmN ; (S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ HilaAlN (K) and ↓ Hil~N (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ HaliylN : (K:) a metaphorical signification, from Hal~u AlEuqodapi [“ the untying of the knot ”] : according to some, meaning what is not forbidden; and therefore including what is disapproved and what is not disapproved: accord. to others, that for which one is not punishable. (TA.) [Hence, maAlN HalaAlK (assumed tropical:) Wealth lawfully acquired. And Aibonu HalaAlK (assumed tropical:) A legitimate son: and an ingenuous, or honest, person. ] And AlHulowu AlHalaAlu (tropical:) Language in which is nothing that induces doubt, or suspicion: (K, TA:) and the man in whom is nothing that induces doubt, or suspicion. (TA in art. Hlw .) And laka ↓ huwa Hil~N (tropical:) It is lawful, allowable, or free, to thee. (TA.) And bil~N ↓ huwa Hil~N , meaning the same; (S;) or w~bil~N ↓ Hil~N ; (K;) and hiya wabil~N ↓ li$aAribK Hil~N : (TA:) see art. bl . ― -b2- (tropical:) A man who has quitted his state of A_iHoraAm ; (S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ muHil~N , (Msb,) and ↓ Hil~N , (S, Msb,) and mina AlA_iHoraAmi ↓ Hil~N ; (S, TA;) or this last signifies one who has not become in that state: (TA:) by rule one should say HaAl~N , which is not used in this sense. (K.) ― -b3- (tropical:) A woman free from any obstacle to marriage, as, for instance, by having accomplished the Eid~ap . (Msb.) ― -b4- See also 5.

definition: A place where a person or party alights, or descends and stops or sojourns or abides or lodges or settles;
sourceDefinition: A place where a person or party alights, or descends and stops or sojourns or abides or lodges or settles; a place of alighting, or descending and stopping &c.; or simply where one takes up his abode, abides, lodges, or settles; (S, Msb, TA;) as also ↓ maHil~N : (Msb:) and ↓ maHal~apN (S, Msb, K) and ↓ Hil~apN , (S,) or ↓ Hal~apN , (K,) signify a [particular, or special,] place of alighting, or descending and stopping &c., (S, Msb, K,) of a people or party: (S, Msb:) the pl. of maHal~N is maHaAl~u ; and the pl. of maHal~apN is maHal~aAtN . sourceDefinition: [ Making one to alight, or descend and stop &c.]. [Hence,] AlmuHil~ataAni (assumed tropical:) The cooking-pot and the hand-mill: and AlmuHil~aAtu the cooking-pot and the hand-mill and the bucket and the knife and the axe and the instrument for striking light ( qad~aAHap , S, or zanod , K) and the water-skin (S, K) and the bowl: (K:) for he who has with him these things alights, or abides, wheresoever he will; but he who has not must be near to persons from whom he may borrow some one or more thereof. (S.) [Hence, also,] taloEapN muHil~apN (assumed tropical:) A tlEp [q. v.] comprising one bayot [or tent ], or two. (O, K.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) [ Making a debt to fall due. ] The Arabs used to say, when they saw the new moon, laA maroHabFA bimuHil~i Ald~ayoni wa muqar~ibi AlA=jaAli (assumed tropical:) [ No welcome be to that which makes the debt to fall due, and makes near the appointed periods! ]. (TA.) ― -b3- See also HalaAlN . ― -b4- Also (assumed tropical:) One with whom it is lawful to fight: (S in art. Hrm :) or whom it is lawful to slay: (TA:) contr. of muHorimN , in the former sense, (S ubi suprà,) or in the latter sense. (TA.) ― -b5- (assumed tropical:) One who has no claim, or covenanted right, to protection, or safeguard, or respect; (S, TA;) contr. of muHorimN , in this sense also. (S.) ― -b6- (assumed tropical:) A man who violates that which is sacred: or who does not hold that there is any sacredness pertaining to the sacred month. (K.) ― -b7- See also 4, last sentence but one.

(Msb.)

definition: A side of anything;
sourceDefinition: A side of anything; originally HawafapN ; (Msb;) and so ↓ HawofN : (TA:) HaAfataAni signifying the two sides of a valley (S, Msb, K) &c.; (K;) i. e., of any other thing: (TA:) pl. HaAfaAtN (Msb, K) and HiyofN , which is irregular, and HiyafN , which is regular, and HawaAy^ifu ; which is extr., like HawaAy^iju , and changed by transposition to HawaAfK , (TA in art. Hyf ,) and [coll. gen. n.] ↓ HaAfN . (Ham p. 159.) It is said in a trad., Ealayokun~a biHaAfaAti AlT~ariyqi [ Keep ye (O women) to the sides of the road ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Also, of the dawaAy^is [or bulls or cows that tread wheat or other grain] (K, TA) in the kudos [or wheat &c. collected together in the place where it is trodden out], (TA,) Such as is, or are, at the extremity, exceeding the others in going round. (K, TA.) -A2- Want: (K:) and hardness, or difficulty, of life; (K, TA;) as also ↓ HawofN . (TA.)

definition: , (S, Msb, Mughnee, K,) indecl.
sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, Mughnee, K,) indecl., (S, Msb,) with damm for its termination, (S, Msb, Mughnee,) as being likened to final words [such as qabolu and baEodu ending a proposition], (S, Mughnee,) because it does not [regularly] occur otherwise than prefixed to a proposition, (S,) for the being prefixed to a proposition is like the not being prefixed to anything, as the consequence of being prefixed, which is the sign of the gen. case, is not apparent: (Mughnee:) and Hayova , (S, Mughnee, K,) also indecl., (S,) with fet-h, (S, Mughnee,) to render the pronunciation more easy, (Mughnee,) because damm with Y is deemed difficult to pronounce: (S:) and Hayovi , (Mughnee, K,) with kesr, accord. to the general rule observed to prevent the concurrence of two quiescent letters: (Mughnee:) and in like manner, Hawovu and Hawova and Hawovi : (Mughnee, TA:) of which forms, Hwv is asserted to be the original; (L;) though Hayovu is more chaste than Hawovu , and is the form used in the Kur-án: (Az and TA in art. Hwv :) but some of the Arabs make Hyv decl.: (Mughnee:) it is an adverbial noun of place, (S, Msb,) a vague adverbial noun of place, (L,) [signifying Where, ] like Hiyna with respect to time: (S, K:) or it is a denotative of place, by general consent: but accord. to Akh it sometimes occurs as denoting time, [signifying when, ] as in the following verse, (Mughnee, TA,) which is the strongest evidence of its use in this sense: (TA:) HayovamaA tasotaqimo yuqad~iro laka A@ll~` hu najaAHFA fiY gaAbiri AlA^azomaAni [ Whenever thou shalt pursue a right course, God will decree thee success in the time to come ]: (Mughnee, TA:) but in most instances it occupies the place of an accus., as an adverbial noun of place; or of a gen., governed by mino , and sometimes by another prep., as in the saying (of Zuheyr, TA in art. q$Em ), ladaY Hayovu A^aloqato raHolahaAA^um~u qa$oEami [ At the place where Calamity, or Fate, has put down her saddle, i. e., made her abode ]: and sometimes it occurs as an objective complement, as it is said to do in Aall~`hu A^aEolamu Hayovu yajoEalu risaAlaAtihi [in the Kur vi. 124], i. e. God is knowing: He knows where to bestow his apostolic commissions; yaEolamu being suppressed, as implied by A^aEolamu ; or A^aEolamu may be rendered by EaAlimN , and so may govern the accus. case. (Mughnee.) Accord. to rule, (Mughnee,) in every instance, (S, Mughnee,) it is prefixed to a proposition, (S, Msb, Mughnee,) nominal, or verbal, but in most cases the latter; (Mughnee;) as in A^aquwmu Hayovu yaquwmu zayodN [ I will stand where Zeyd shall stand ]; and Hayovu takuwnu A^akuwnu [ Where thou shalt be, I will be ]; (S;) and jalasotu Hayovu zayodFA A^araAhu [ I sat where I saw Zeyd ], the accus. case being preferred in an instance like this; (Mughnee;) and A*ohabo Hayovu $y^ota [ Go thou whither thou wilt. ] (Msb in art. Hayn .) You should not say Hayovu zayodN [alone]: (S:) or it occurs prefixed to a single word in poetry; (Msb, Mughnee;) as in the saying, wanaToEunuhumo taHota AlkulaY baEoda Darobihimo bibiyDi AlmawaADiY Hayovu laY~i AlEamaAy^imi [ And we pierce them beneath the kidneys, after smiting them, with the sharp swords, where the turbans are wound ]; (Mughnee;) but this is irregular; (Msb, Mughnee;) though Ks holds it to be regular. (Mughnee.) Lh relates, on the authority of Ks, that some make Hyv to govern a noun in the gen. case, as in the saying, A^amaA taraY Hayovu suhayolK TaAliEaA [ Seest thou not where Canopus is, rising? ]: but he says that this is not of respectable authority: (L:) some write Hayova suhayolK : and some, Hayovu suhayolN , [which is the common reading, shyl being an inchoative, and] the enunciative, mawojuwdN , being suppressed. (Mughnee.) Abu-l-Fet-h says that he who prefixes Hyv to a single word makes it declinable. (Mughnee.) [Accord. to Fei,] BenooTemeem say Hayova when it occupies the place of an accus., as in the phrase, qumo Hayova yaquwmu zayodN [ Stand thou where Zeyd shall stand ]. (Msb.) Ks says, I have heard among Benoo-Temeem, of Benoo-Yarbooa and Tuheiyeh, those who say Hayova in every case, when it occupies the place of a gen., and that of an accus., and that of a nom.; saying mino Hayova laAyaEolamuwna [ Whence they know not ], and Hayova A@lotaqayonaA [ Where we met ]: and he says also, I have heard some of Benu-l-HárithIbn-Asad-Ibn-El-Hárith-Ibn-Thaalabeh, and all Benoo-Fak'as, say Hayovi when it occupies the place of a gen., and Hayova when it occupies the place of an accus.; saying mino Hayovi laA yaEolamuwna , and Hayova A@lotaqayonaA . (L.) Sometimes the proposition after Hyv commences with A_in~a , as in Aijoliso Hayovu A_in~a zayodFA jaAlisN [ Sit thou where Zeyd is sitting ]. (K in art. A^n , and IAk p. 92.) ― -b2- It sometimes comprises the meanings of two adverbial nouns of place, as when you say, Hayovu Eabodu A@ll~`hi qaAEidN zayodN qaAy^imN [ Where' Abd-Allah is sitting, there Zeyd is standing ]. (AHeyth, L.) ― -b3- The restrictive maA ( maA kaAf~apN ) is sometimes affixed to it, and in this case it implies a conditional meaning, [signifying Wherever, or wheresoever, and, accord. to Akh, whenever, or whensoever, ] (Mughnee, TA,) and renders two verbs mejzoom, (Mughnee,) as in the saying, HayovumaA tajoliso A^ajoliso [ Wherever thou shalt sit, I will sit ], (S,) and in the first of the verses cited above: (Mughnee, TA:) it is not [properly, though it is sometimes improperly,] used as a conditional without mA . (S.) ― -b4- [It is also used, in scientific and other post-classical works, in senses different from those explained above. Thus, mino Hayovu is used to signify As to, or in respect of: so in the phrase mino Hayovu All~afoZi waAlmaEonaY As to, or in respect of, the word and the meaning. Also As, or considered as, absolutely, or abstractedly: so in the phrase mino Hayovu huwa , or mino Hayovu huwa huwa , As, or considered as, such, absolutely, or abstractedly; and AlA_inosaAnu mino Hayovu huwa A_inosaAnN Man, as, or considered as, man, absolutely, or abstractedly. And As, meaning considered merely or only or simply as: so in the saying, AlA_inosaAnu mino Hayovu A_in~ahu yaSiH~u watazuwlu Eanohu Als~iH~apu mawoDuwEu AlT~ib~i Man, as, or considered merely or only or simply as, being healthy and ceasing to be healthy, is the object of therapeutics. And As, meaning since, or because: so in the saying, Aln~aAru mino Hayovu A_in~ahaA HaAr~apN tusax~inu AlmaA='a Fire, as, or since, or because, it is hot, heats water. biHayovu is also vulgarly used in this sense. And correctly as meaning So that; so as that; in such a state, or condition, that: often syn. with Hat~aY .]

(AHeyth, L.) ― -b3- The restrictive maA ( maA kaAf~apN ) is sometimes affixed to it, and in this case it implies a conditional meaning, [signifying Wherever, or wheresoever, and, accord. to Akh, whenever, or whensoever, ] (Mughnee, TA,) and renders two verbs mejzoom, (Mughnee,) as in the saying, HayovumaA tajoliso A^ajoliso [ Wherever thou shalt sit, I will sit ], (S,) and in the first of the verses cited above: (Mughnee, TA:) it is not [properly, though it is sometimes improperly,] used as a conditional without mA . (S.) ― -b4- [It is also used, in scientific and other post-classical works, in senses different from those explained above. Thus, mino Hayovu is used to signify As to, or in respect of: so in the phrase mino Hayovu All~afoZi waAlmaEonaY As to, or in respect of, the word and the meaning. Also As, or considered as, absolutely, or abstractedly: so in the phrase mino Hayovu huwa , or mino Hayovu huwa huwa , As, or considered as, such, absolutely, or abstractedly; and AlA_inosaAnu mino Hayovu huwa A_inosaAnN Man, as, or considered as, man, absolutely, or abstractedly. And As, meaning considered merely or only or simply as: so in the saying, AlA_inosaAnu mino Hayovu A_in~ahu yaSiH~u watazuwlu Eanohu Als~iH~apu mawoDuwEu AlT~ib~i Man, as, or considered merely or only or simply as, being healthy and ceasing to be healthy, is the object of therapeutics. And As, meaning since, or because: so in the saying, Aln~aAru mino Hayovu A_in~ahaA HaAr~apN tusax~inu AlmaA='a Fire, as, or since, or because, it is hot, heats water. biHayovu is also vulgarly used in this sense. And correctly as meaning So that; so as that; in such a state, or condition, that: often syn. with Hat~aY .]

sourceDefinition: [a coll. gen. n.,] a word of well-known meaning, (Msb,) [i.e., Beads; ] what are strung: (S:) a thing that is hung [or rather things that are hung ] upon the neck, made of coloured stone, red and green: (Har p. 431:) or gems, or similar stones, both good and bad: (JK:) [also factitious gems, and the like: (see fusayofisaA='u as explained in the K &c:)] n. un. xarazapN : (S, Msb:) the latter signifying [a single bead;] what is strung: (K:) and also, (i.e. the latter,) a gem, or precious stone, (K, TA,) such [for instance] as is set in a ring, whether good or bad: (TA:) pl. of the latter, xarazaAtN . (TA.) Hence, xarazaAtu Almaliki , (S, K,) and Almuloki , (S, A,) The gems of the king's crown: when the king had reigned a year, a xarazap was added to his crown, in order that the number of the years of his reign might be known: (S, K:) such is said to have been the case. (S.) You say, A^uwtiYa xarazaAti Almuloki sit~iyna Hij~apF (tropical:) [meaning He reigned sixty years: lit., he received the gems of the crown sixty years ]. (A.) ― -b2- xarazapu AlEayoni signifies The Hadaqap [or lens ] of the eye. (TA in art. Hdq ) ― -b3- And xarazN is also applied to The small shells called wadaE . (S* and K* and TA in art. wdE .) ― -b4- It also signifies (tropical:) The vertebræ of the back, (S, A, TA,) and of the neck: each one is called xarazapN : which latter is also explained as meaning (tropical:) what is between two vertebræ. (TA.)

definition: and ↓ xayozalaY A certain mode of walking, with a looseness of the joints;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ xayozalaY A certain mode of walking, with a looseness of the joints; like xawozaraY and xayozaraY : (S:) or a heavy, or sluggish, manner of walking; as also ↓ xayozalN : (K:) the dual of xawozalaY [to which that of xayozalaY is similar] is xawozalaAni . (TA.)

[Hence,] xaTama A^anofahu (tropical:) [ He branded him with disgrace; ] he made disgrace to cleave to him manifestly. (TA.) And xaTamahu biAll~awomi (tropical:) [ He branded him with blame ]; and Ea*arahu [i. e. bAllwm signifies the same]. (TA.) ― -b3- He attached the zimaAm [or xiTaAm , q. v.,] to him; namely, a camel: (S:) or xaTamahu biAlxiTaAmi , (K,) aor. and inf. n. as above, (TA,) he put the xiTaAm upon his nose; as also bihi ↓ xT~mhu : (K:) [but the latter verb seems to be more properly used in relation to a number of camels:] or the former, (K,) or simply xaTamahu , and ↓ xT~mhu , (TA,) he made a cut, or notch, in his nose, ( Haz~aA^anofahu , so in the K accord. to the TA,) not deep, (TA,) or he drew his nose [ down ], ( jar~a A^anofahu , so in my MS. copy of the K and in the CK,) in order to put upon it the xiTaAm . (K, TA.) ― -b4- [Hence,] (assumed tropical:) He withheld him, or prevented him, from going forth [&c.]. (TA.) And xaTamahu biAlkalaAmi (tropical:) He overcame him, or subdued him, by speech, and prevented him from speaking, (K, TA,) and from answering, or replying. (TA.) ― -b5- xaTama Alkalimapa , inf. n. as above, (tropical:) He made the word, or saying, valid and strong; alluding to prudence and precaution as to what one utters. (TA.) ― -b6- xaTama A^umuwrFA (tropical:) He conducted, or managed, affairs. (TA.) ― -b7- xaTama Alqawosa biAlwatari , inf. n. xaTomN and xiTaAmN , (tropical:) He suspended the bow by the suspensory called watarN and xiTaAmN . (AHn, K, TA.) sourceDefinition: The muzzle, i. e. the fore part of the nose and mouth, of a dAb~ap [i. e. beast], (JK, S, Msb, K, TA,) whatever it be, (S, Msb,) as a dog, and a camel, but originally of a beast of prey, and of a sheep or goat: (TA:) or, of a beast of prey, i. q. xuroTuwmN : (IAar, TA:) or, as some say, of a beast of prey, [the lip, i. e.] what corresponds to the jaHofalap of the horse: (TA:) or of a camel, the nose. (Mgh.) And (tropical:) The bill, or beak, of a bird, (JK, S, K, TA,) whatever it be, (JK, S,) as a hawk, or falcon, (JK,) and a qaTaAp . (TA.) And of a man, (tropical:) The nose; (K;) as also ↓ maxoTimN (JK, S, Msb, K, TA) and ↓ mixoTamN ; (K, TA;) pl. maxaATimu : (JK, S, Msb, K:) or the fore part of the nose: (Har p. 433:) and the ↓ mxTm is also of a camel. (IAth, TA.) Also, of a man, (tropical:) The fore part of the face. (TA.) ― -b2- xaTomu All~ayoli (tropical:) The first approach of night: like as one says A^anofu All~ayoli . (TA.) ― -b3- See also xiTaAmN . -A2- A thing, an affair, or a business, of magnitude. (IAar, Th, K.) It is related in a trad. that Mohammad promised a certain man to go forth to him, and delayed to do so; and when he went forth, he said to him, $agalaniY xaTomN , meaning A thing, &c., of magnitude [ occupied me so as to divert me ]; as though the m were a substitute for b : (IAar, Th, TA:) but IAth says that it may mean (assumed tropical:) a thing, &c., that withheld me, or prevented me, [see 1,] from going forth. (TA.)

definition: [ A kind of halter for a camel;
sourceDefinition: [ A kind of halter for a camel; a cord of which one end is fastened round the nose and jaws of a camel; accord. to J,] i. q. zimaAmN : (S:) [ but the following explanations are more correct: ] a certain thing well known; so called because [ a portion of ] it lies upon [or surrounds ] the fore part of the nose and the nouth of the camel: (Msb:) or anything that is put upon the nose of the camel in order that he may be led thereby: (M, K:) or a cord, or rope, which is put upon the neck of the camel, and folded [for yusam~aY , in my copy of the work from which this is taken, I read yuvonaY , as in another explanation, below,] upon, or over, his nose: (Mgh:) or a cord, or rope, which is attached to an iron that surrounds the nose and jaws [ of the camel ]: (JK:) or any cord, or rope, that is suspended upon the throat of the camel and then tied upon, or over, his nose, whether of skin or of wool or of fibres of the palm-tree or of hemp: (ISh, TA:) but if of plaited leather, it is said to be called jariyrN : (TA:) or the xTAm of the camel is a cord, or rope, of fibres of the palm-tree, or of [ goats' ] hair, or of flax, at one end of which is put a ring, then the other end is tied to it, [i. e. to the rope, as the relative pronoun in the original shows, or to some part of it,] so that it becomes like a ring [or loop ], then it is put upon the neck of the camel, and then it is folded upon, or over, his nose: what is put in the nose, [attached to a ring, or the like, therein,] and is slender, is termed zimaAmN : (IAth, TA:) pl. xuTumN . (Msb, K.) manaEa xiTaAmahu , said of a camel, means He refused to have his xTAm put upon him. (TA.) And tazaw~aja EalaY xiTaAmK means (assumed tropical:) He married two wives, so that they became like a xiTaAm to him. (TA.) ― -b2- (assumed tropical:) A brand, or mark made with a hot iron, upon the nose of a camel; (K;) as also ↓ xaTomN : it (the xTAm ) spreads upon the camel's two cheeks: so says Aboo-'Alee, in the “ Tedhkireh: ” (TA:) or such a mark upon the side ( EuroD , in the CK EaroD ,) of his face, extending to the cheek, (En-Nadr, K, TA,) in the form of a line: (En-Nadr, TA:) sometimes the camel is branded with one such mark, and sometimes with two; and one says jamalN xiTaAmK ↓ maxoTuwmu or xiTaAmayoni , making mxTwm to govern the gen. case as a prefixed noun; (En-Nadr, K, TA;) and bihi xiTaAmN and xiTaAmaAn . (En-Nadr, TA.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) The rope of a bucket. (TA.) ― -b4- (tropical:) The suspensory of a bow. (AHn, K, TA.) And (assumed tropical:) The string of a bow. (K, TA.)

definition: signifies The act of measuring;
sourceDefinition: signifies The act of measuring; or determining the measure, proportion, or the like, of a thing; and the making a thing by measure, or according to the measure of another thing; or proportioning a thing to another thing; syn. taqodiyrN : (S, Msb, K, TA, and Bd in ii. 19:) this is the primary meaning. (Msb, TA, and Bd ubi suprà.) You say, xalaqa AlA^adiymi , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (S, TA,) inf. n. xaloqN (JK, S, Msb, K) and xaloqapN , (K,) He measured, or proportioned, ( qad~ara ,) the hide, and sewed it: (K:) or he measured, or proportioned, ( qd~r ,) the hide, (JK, S, Msb, K,) limaA yuriydu [ for, or to, that which he desired to make of it], (JK, * TA,) or lils~iqaA='i [ for, or to, the skin for water or milk that he desired to make], (Msb,) before cutting it; (S, K, TA;) he measured it ( qaAsahu ) to cut from it a water-bag, or a water-skin, or a boot: (TA:) and in like manner, xalaqa Aln~iTaEa he measured, &c., the nTE [q. v.]: when one cuts it, one says, faraAhu . (K.) And xalaqa Aln~aEola He determined the measure of the sandal, or proportioned it; ( qad~arahaA ;) and made it by measure. (Ksh and Bd in ii. 19.) Hence the saying of Zuheyr, (S,) praising Herim Ibn-Sinán, (TA,) walaA^anota taforiY maA xalaqota wabaEo Du Alqawomi yaxoluqu vum~a laA yaforiY In the preceding quotation, the final character of the first line and initial character of the second are missing in the original text. [(assumed tropical:) And thou indeed cuttest what thou hast measured; but some of the people measure, then will not cut ]: (S, TA:) i. e., when thou determinest upon a thing thou executest it; but others determine upon that which they do not execute. (TA.) And El-Hajjáj said, maA xalaqotu A_il~aA qarayotu waEadotu A_il~aA wafayotu [(assumed tropical:) I have not measured unless I have afterwards cut, and I have not promised unless I have afterwards performed ]. (S.) A^axoluqu lakumo mina AlT~iyni kahayoy^api AlT~ayori , in the Kur iii. 43, means I will form for you, (Jel,) or I will make according to its proper measure ( A^uqad~iru ) for you, (Ksh, Bd,) and will form, (Bd,) of clay, a thing like the form of the bird, or of birds. (Ksh, Bd, Jel.) ― -b2- [Hence,] it signifies also The bringing a thing into existence according to a certain measure, or proportion, and so as to make it equal [ to another thing ], or uniform [ therewith ]: (Ksh and Bd in ii. 19:) or the originating, or producing, [a thing] after a pattern, or model, which one has devised, not after the similitude of anything preexisting: this is another meaning which it has in the [classical] language of the Arabs. (TA.) As the act of God, it signifies The originating, or bringing into being or existence, anything, not after the similitude of anything pre-existing: (TA:) [and the creating a thing; and thus it is generally best rendered; as meaning the bringing into existence from a state of non-existence: for] xalaqa A@ll~`hu Al$~aYo'a , inf. n. xaloqN , means God brought the thing into existence (Mgh, * TA) after it had not been: (TA:) [or xaloqN , as the act of God, signifies the creating out of nothing: for it is said that] A^uEobuduwA rab~akumu A@l~a*iY xalaqakumo , in the Kur ii. 19, means [ Serve ye your Lord ] who brought you into existence when ye were nothing. (Jel. [But in other passages of the Kur (vi. 2 &c.) it is said that God created ( xalaqa ) mankind of clay.]) Accord. to the A, xalaqa A@ll~`hu Alxaloqa is a tropical phrase, meaning (tropical:) God brought into existence the creation, or created beings, or mankind, according to a predetermination ( taqodiyr ) required by wisdom. (TA.) You say, h`*ihi xaliyqatuhu Al~atiY xuliqa EalayohaA and xuliqahaA and Al~atiY xuliqa : see xuluqN . (Lh.) ― -b3- [Hence, also,] xalaqa , (S, Msb, K, TA,) inf. n. xaloqN , (TA,) (tropical:) He fabricated speech, or a saying or sentence, &c.: (K, * TA:) (tropical:) he forged (S, Msb, K, TA) a saying, (Msb,) or a lie, or a falsehood; (S, K, TA;) as also ↓ Axtlq (S, Msb, K) and ↓ txl~q . (S, K.) The Arabs say, Had~avanaA fulaAnN biA^aHaAdiyvi Alxaloqi (tropical:) Such a one related to us fictitious tales or stories, such as are deemed pretty, or such as are told by night [ for entertainment ]. (TA.) And it is said in the Kur [xxvi. 137], accord. to one reading, A_ino h`*aA A_il~aA xaloqu AlA^aw~aliyna , meaning (tropical:) This is nought but the lying, and forging, of the ancients. (TA.) And in the same [xxxviii. 6], ↓ A_ino h`*aA A_il~aA A@xotilaAqN (tropical:) This is nought but forging, and lying. (TA.) ― -b4- xalaqahu , (K,) inf. n. xaloqN , (TA,) also signifies He made it smooth; (K;) and so ↓ xl~qhu ; namely, an arrow, (S,) [and any other thing; for] of anything that has been made smooth one says, xul~iqa : (TA:) he made it equable, or even; namely, wood, or a stick; and so ↓ xl~qhu , (K,) inf. n. taxoliyqN . (TA.) -A2- xaluqato , inf. n. xalaAqapN , said of a woman, (JK, K,) She had [ a goodly ] body and make: (JK:) or she was, or became, goodly in make, or well made. (K. [In the CK, instead of Hasuna xaloquhaA , is put Hasuna xuluquhA , meaning She was, or became, good in nature, &c.]) ― -b2- And xaliqa , aor. , (JK, K,) inf. n. xalaqN ; (JK, S; *) and xaluqa , aor. , (K,) inf. n. xuluwqapN (TA) [and xalaAqapN , and perhaps xuloqapN q. v. infrà]; It (a thing) was, or became, smooth, (JK, K, TA,) and equable, or even. (TA.) [See also 12. And it seems that one says, xaliqati AlS~axorapu , inf. n. xalaqN , q. v. infrà, meaning The rock was free from crack or fracture. ] ― -b3- And xaluqa , (JK, S, Msb, K,) aor. ; (K;) and xaliqa , aor. ; and xalaqa , aor. ; (K;) inf. n. (of the first, JK, S) xuluwqapN (JK, S, K) and xalaAqapN (JK, TA) and [of the second] xalaqN (K) and [of the third] xuluwqN ; (JK, TA;) It (a garment) was, or became, old, and worn out; as also ↓ Axlq , (JK, S, Msb,) inf. n. A_ixolaAqN ; (JK, TA;) and ↓ Axlwlq . (TA.) [Hence,] diybaAjuhu ↓ Axlq [lit.] His face became worn out; meaning (tropical:) it became used for mean service [ so that it lost its grace, or was disgraced, ] by his begging. (Har p. 476. [See also 4 below.]) [Hence also,] $abaAbahu ↓ Axlq (assumed tropical:) His youth declined, or departed. (TA.) ― -b4- And xaluqa , (S, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. xalAqapN , (Ham p. 522,) He was, or became, xaliyq , i. e. jadiyr [meaning adapted or disposed by nature, apt, meet, &c.: see xaliyqN , below]. (S, K.) You say, xaluqa l*`lika [and bi*`lika (see xaliyqN ) He was, or became, adapted, disposed, &c., for that ]; as though he were one of those in whom that was reckoned to be, and in whom the symptoms, signs, or tokens, thereof were seen. (S.) [And xaluqa A^ano yafoEala *`lika and biA^ano yfEl *lk and liA^ano yfEl *lk and mano A^ano yfEl *lk He was, or became, adapted, &c., to do that: see xaliyqN . And xaluqa may signify also It was, or became, probable; or likely to happen or be, or to have happened or been: see, again, xaliyqN .]

(S, Msb, K.) [Hence,] Axlq Ald~ahoru Al$~aYo'a (assumed tropical:) Time wore out, or wasted, the thing. (TA.) [Hence also,] one says to the beggar, A^axolaqota wajohaka (tropical:) (TA) [lit. And some say, Axlqhu xalaqFA He gave him an old and worn-out garment. (TA.) ― -b3- And A_ixolaAqN Alv~awobi also signifies The cutting out of the garment: whence the saying, to UmmKhálid, A^aboliY waA^axoliqiY [ Wear out, and cut out new]; or, as some relate it, waA^axolifiY , i. e., “ and replace, ” which is the more likely. (TA.) -A3- maA A^axolaqahu and A^axoliqo bihi [have both of the following significations; though it is said that] the former signifies How likely is he, or it! (JK, TA;) and the latter, How well adapted or disposed, or how apt, meet, suited, suitable, fitted, fit, competent, or proper, or how worthy, is he, or it! i. q. A^ajodiro bihi and A^aHori bihi . (TA. [See 4 in arts. jdr and HrY .])

sourceDefinition: inf. n. of xalaqa . (JK, S, Msb, K, &c.) You say rajulN taAm~u Alxaloqi [ A man complete, or perfect, in respect of make, or proportion, &c.]. (S, K. * [See also xiloqapN .]) [In this and similar instances,] Alxaloq signifies The fashion of the outer man, and its [ peculiar ] qualities and attributes; like as Alxuluqu signifies “ the fashion of the inner man, ” &c. (TA.) ― -b2- Alxaloqu is also used in the sense of ↓ Almaxoluwqu [meaning What is created; the creature ]: (TA, and Bd in xxiii. 17, &c.:) [and, collectively, the creation; as meaning the beings, or things, that are created; ] all created things: (Bd ubi suprà, &c.:) and [particularly] mankind; as also ↓ Alxliyqapu : (S, * K:) and mankind and the jinn, or genii, and others: (Jel in lv. 9, &c.:) and ↓ Alxliyqapu and [its pl.] xalaAy^iqu signify the same: you say, humo xaliyqapu A@ll~`hi and also humo xalqu A@ll~`hi [ They are the creatures of God ]: Alxaloqu being originally an inf. n.: (S, TA:) and Lh mentions [an instance of its having a pl., in] the saying, laA waA@l~a*iY xalaqa Alxuluwqa maA faEalotu ka*aA , meaning [ No, by Him who created ] all creatures, [ I did not such a thing. ] (TA.) In the saying, falayugay~irun~a xaloqa A@ll~`hi , in the Kur [iv. 118, lit. And they shall alter the creature of God ], some say that castration is meant: (TA: [and Bd includes, with this, other unnatural actions:]) or the meaning is, the religion of God; (Bd, Jel, TA;) accord. to El-Hasan and Mujáhid. (TA.) And laA tabodiyla lixaloqi A@ll~`hi , in the Kur [xxx. 29], means, accord. to Katádeh, [ There shall be no changing, or altering, ] of the religion of God. (TA.) ― -b3- xaloqN also signifies Anything made smooth. (TA.) [See also muxal~aqN .]

definition: inf. n. of xaliqa : as such, signifying The being smooth [&c.]. (JK, S. *) [As such also,] in a rock, Freedom from crack or fracture. (S, K.) ― -b2- [And, as such,] The being old, and worn out. (K.)...
sourceDefinition: inf. n. of xaliqa : as such, signifying The being smooth [&c.]. (JK, S. *) [As such also,] in a rock, Freedom from crack or fracture. (S, K.) ― -b2- [And, as such,] The being old, and worn out. (K.) ― -b3- [Hence, used as an epithet,] Old, and worn out: (S, Msb, K:) [and as an epithet in which the quality of a subst. is predominant; meaning an old and worn-out garment or piece of cloth: ] pl. xuloqaAnN (S, K) and A^axolaAqN . (S, * K, * TA.) And [as an epithet] it is masc. and fem.; (S, K;) because it is originally an inf. n., the inf. n. of A^axolaqu meaning “ smooth, ” (S,) [or rather of xaliqa meaning “ it was, or became, old, and worn out; ” although it has pls.; and] IB mentions an instance of its dual, xalaqaAni : (TA:) Ks says, We have not heard them say, xalaqapN in any instance: (Lh, TA:) Fr says that it is without p [as a fem. epithet] because it was originally used as a prefixed noun; for one said, A^aEoTiniY xalaqa jub~atika and xalaqa EimaAmatika [lit. meaning Give thou to me what is old, and worn out, of thy jb~p and of thy turban ]; but Ez-Zejjájee says that this is nought. (TA.) You say vawobN xalaqN [ An old and worn-out garment or piece of cloth ], and miloHafapN xalaqN [ an old and worn-out outer wrapping garment ]: (S:) also rum~apN xalaqN [ an old and worn-out piece of rope ]: and daArN xalaqN [ an old and decayed house ]: and jisomN xalaqN [ an old and wasted body ]. (TA.) One says also vawobN A^axolaAqN , meaning A garment, or piece of cloth, altogether, or wholly, old and worn out; (Fr, S, K;) every portion of it being xalaq ; (Fr;) like as they said buromapN A^aEo$aArN &c.: (S:) and in like manner, mulaA='apN A^axolaAqN . (IAar.) And Ks mentions the saying, A^aSobaHato viyaAbuhumo xuloqaAnFA wa xalaquhumo jududFA [ Their garments became old, and worn out; and their old and worn-out garments became replaced by new ]; with the sing. [in the latter clause] in the place of the pl. xuloqaAn : (TA:) or jududFA may be here put for jadiydFA . (L in art. jd .) In the phrase ↓ miloHafapN xulayoqN [ An outer wrapping garment that is a little, or somewhat, old, and worn out ], the dim. is without p because it is [the dim. of] an epithet [applied without p to a fem. n.], and p is not affixed to the dims. of epithets [of this kind]: it is like nuSayufN dim. of naSafN an epithet applied to a woman. (S, K. * [See Lumsden's Arab. Gram. p. 623: but some of the grammarians consider these instances as anomalous.]) ― -b4- baAEahu biyEapa Alxalaqi , and bayoEa *iY Alxalaqi , the latter as used by a poet, [lit. He bought it, or sold it, (app. the former,) as one buys, or sells, the old and worn-out garment, like as we say “ dogcheap, ” and “ cheap as dirt ”], are phrases mentioned, but not explained, by IAar, who cites the following saying: A^aboligo fazaArapa A^an~iY qado $arayotu lahaA majoda AlHayaApi bisayofiY bayoEa *iY Alxalaqi [app. meaning Tell thou Fezárah that I have purchased for them life-long glory (lit. the glory of life ), with my sword, as cheaply, i. e as easily, as one purchases the old and worn-out garment ]. (TA.) ― -b5- saHaAbapN xalaqapN : see the next paragraph.

sourceDefinition: (S, Msb, K) and ↓ xuloqN (S, K) A nature; or a natural, a native, or an innate, disposition or temper or the like; syn. sajiy~apN , (S, Msb, K, TA,) and TaboEN ; (K, TA;) of which one is created: (TA:) and ↓ xiloqapN signifies [the same; i. e.] the fiTorapN [or nature, &c.,] (S, Msb, K, TA) of which a man is created; (TA;) like [ xuluqN and] ↓ xuloqN : (K, TA: [in the CK, erroneously, xaloq :]) and ↓ xaliyqapN [also] signifies [ the same; i. e.] the TabiyEap [or nature, &c.,] (S, K, TA) with which a man is created: (TA:) the proper signification of xuluqN is [the moral character; or] the fashion of the inner man; i. e. his mind, or soul, and its peculiar qualities and attributes; like as xaloqN signifies the “ fashion of the outer man, and its [peculiar] qualities and attributes: ” it signifies also custom or habit [as being a second nature ]: (TA:) and, as also ↓ xuloqN , [which is merely a contraction thereof, and therefore identical with it in all its senses,] manliness; syn. muruwo'apN : and religion: (IAar, K:) the pl. is A^axolaAqN only: (TA:) [this is often used as signifying morals: and ethics: ] and the pl. of ↓ xaliyqapN in the sense explained above [said in Har p. 193 to be that of xuluqN ] is xalaAy^iqN . (S.) It is said in a trad., layosa $aYo'N fiY AlmiyzaAni A^avoqala mino Husoni Alxuluqi [ Nothing is heavier in the balance in which good and evil will be weighed than goodness of the moral character, &c.] (TA.) And one says, EalayohaA ↓ Al~atiY xuliqa ↓ h`*ihi xaliyqatuhu and ↓ xuliqahaA and ↓ Al~atiY xuliqa This is his nature, &c., of which he was created. (Lh.) And ↓ A_in~ahu lakariymu Alxaliyqapi Verily he is generous in respect of nature, &c. (AZ.) And SaAra *`lika lahu xuluqFA That became to him [ a second nature, a habit, or] a thing to which he was habituated. (TA.) It is said in the Kur [xxvi. 137], A_ino h`*aA A_il~aA xuluqu AlA^aw~aliyna This is nought but a custom of the ancients. (TA.) And in the same [lxviii. 4], wa A_in~aka laEalaY xuluqK EaZiymK And verily thou art of a great religion. (Jel, TA.) And in a trad. of 'Áïsheh, kaAna xuluquhu AlqaroA=na , meaning That whereto he clung was the Kur-án, with its rules of discipline and its command and its prohibitions, and the excellences and beauties and gracious things comprised in it. (TA.) ― -b2- nawomapu Alxulqi [i. e. Alxuluqi or ↓ Alxuloqi ] The sleep of midday, which was prescribed by the Prophet. (Har p. 223. [See also HumoqN and xuroqN .])

definition: , applied to a man, (S, TA,) Perfect, or complete, in make;
sourceDefinition: , applied to a man, (S, TA,) Perfect, or complete, in make; (TA;) as also ↓ muxotalaqN : (Ham p. 561:) or perfect, or complete, in make, and just in proportion; (S, TA;) and so ↓ the latter; (S, K, TA; [in the CK, erroneously, muxotaliq ; in the TA expressly said to be of the pass. form;]) fem. of the former with p : (TA:) or ↓ both signify goodly, or beautiful, in make: or the former is not applied to a man; but ↓ each, with p , signifies a woman having [ a goodly ] body and make: (TA, in which this signification is said to be tropical:) and xaliyqN and xaliyqapN are alike, (JK, TA,) accord. to Lh, (TA,) in this last sense: (JK:) or the former of these two may be pl. [or coll. gen. n.] of the latter, like as $aEiyrN is of $aEiyrapN : (TA:) and ↓ muxotalaqN signifies anything just in proportion: (IF, TA:) ↓ muxal~aqN , also, signifies perfect, or complete, in make; applied to a camel ( jml ): (TA:) [or jml , here may be a mistranscription for Hamol ; for] ↓ muDogapN muxal~aqapN signifies [ a fœtus when it has become like a lump of flesh ] perfect, or complete, in make; (Fr, S, K;) so in the Kur xxii. 5; (Fr, TA;) or of which the make has become apparent. (IAar, TA.) ― -b2- Also Adapted or disposed [ by nature ], apt, meet, suited, suitable, fitted, fit, proper, competent, or worthy; (KL, PS;) syn. jadiyrN (S, K) and HariY~N (TA) [and HaqiyqN &c.: pl. xulaqaA='u , and Freytag adds xuluqN ]. You say, fulaAnN xaliyqN lika*aA , i. e. jadiyrN bihi [ Such a one is adapted or disposed by nature, &c., for such a thing ]; as though he were one of those in whom that was reckoned to be, and in whom the symptoms, signs, or tokens, thereof were seen. (S.) [And huwa xaliyqN liloxayori He is adapted or disposed by nature to good; i. e., to be, or to do, or to effect, or to produce, what is good. ] And A_in~ahu laxaliyqN A^ano yafoEala *`lika and biA^ano yfEl *lk and liA^ano yfEl *lk and mno A^ano yfEl *lk [ Verily he is adapted or disposed &c. for doing that; or worthy to do it ]: so says Lh: and he adds that the Arabs say, yaA xaliyqu bi*`lika , using the nom. case; and yaA xaliyqFA bi*`lika , using the accus. case; [the latter being the usual form; both meaning O thou who art adapted or disposed &c. for that; ] but ISd says, I know not the reason of this. (TA.) And li*aAka ↓ h`*aA maxolaqapN , i. e. majodarapN lahu [ This is one that is adapted or disposed &c. for that ]: (S, K: *) and laka ↓ h`*aA AlA^amoru maxolaqapN [ This affair, or thing, is one that is adapted &c. for thee ]: and mino *`lika ↓ A_in~ahu maxolaqapN [ Verily it is adapted &c. for that ]: like majodarapN and maHoraApN and maqomanapN : and in like manner one says of two, and of more than two, and of a feminine: so says Lh. (TA.) [↓ maxolaqapN properly signifies A place, and hence a thing, an affair, and a person, adapted or disposed &c.: it is of the same class as maEosaApN and maZin~apN and may^in~apN .] xaliyqN also signifies Habituated, or accustomed. (PS, TA. *) And one says, A_in~ahu laxaliyqN , i. e. laHariY~N , meaning Verily it is probable; or likely to happen or be, or to have happened or been. (TA.) And huwa xaliyqN lahu He, or it, is like to him, or it. (JK, TA.) ― -b3- saHaAbapN xaliyqapN : see xaliqN . ― -b4- [See also xaliyqapN , which, in several senses, is a fem. epithet used as a subst.]

definition: Smooth: (JK, K:) smooth and solid;
sourceDefinition: Smooth: (JK, K:) smooth and solid; (S, K, TA;) applied in this sense to anything: (TA:) smooth and firm: (JK:) fem. xaloqaA='u . (JK, S, K.) You say HajarN A^axolaqu Stone that is smooth (K, TA) and solid, upon which nothing makes an impression. (TA.) And SaxorapN xaloqaA='u A rock, or great mass of stone, smooth (K, TA) and solid: (TA:) or free from crack and fracture. (S, K, TA.) And firosinN xaloqaA='u A camel's foot in which is no crack. (Ibn-'Abbád, K.) And haDobapN xaloqaA='u [ A hill, or the like, ] destitute of herbage or vegetation. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] (assumed tropical:) Poor; syn. faqiyrN . (K.) You say rajulN A^axolaqu mina AlmaAli (assumed tropical:) A man destitute of property. (TA.) And it is said in a trad., layosa Alfaqiyra faqiyru AlmaAli A_in~amaA Alfaqiyru AlA^axolaqu Alkasobi , i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ The poor in respect of property is not the poor the poor is only ] he who has no good deeds for which he will be rewarded in the world to come. (TA, in two places.) ― -b3- AlA^axolaqu also signifies The exterior of a horse's hoof. (JK.) ― -b4- And xaloqaA='u , (JK, S, K,) applied to a woman, (JK, S,) Impervia coëunti; (S, K, TA;) as also ↓ xul~aqN . (Ibn-'Abbád, K.) ― -b5- See also xaliqN . ― -b6- And AlxaloqaA='u [used as a subst.] The sky; because of its smoothness and evenness. (TA.) ― -b7- And The side of a camel &c. (K.) One says also, Darabotu xaloqaA='a janobihi (K, TA [in the CK ElY xaloqaA'a janobihi ]) I struck the outer part of his side. (TA.) ― -b8- And The interior (Lth, K, TA) and smooth part (Lth, TA,) of the gaAr , (K,) i. e., of [the upper part of the interior of the mouth, or] what is termed AlgaAru AlA^aEolaY ; (Lth, TA;) as also ↓ AlxulayoqaA='u [the dim. of AlxaloqaA='u ]: (Lth, K, TA:) or both signify what appears of the gAr : and the dim. form is that which is predominant in this case. (TA.) ― -b9- And The part of the forehead that is even (JK, K, TA) and smooth; (TA;) as also ↓ AlxulayoqaA='u . (JK, K, TA.) One says, suHibuwA EalaY xaloqaAwaAti jibaAhihimo [ They were dragged along upon the even and smooth parts of their foreheads ]. (TA [in which this is said to be tropical]) ― -b10- Alfarasi ↓ xulayoqaA='u That [ part ] of the horse which is like the Eironiyn [or upper part of the nose ] of man; (S, K;) the part where the forehead of the horse meets the narrow portion of the bone of the nose: AO says that the xulayoqaAwaAni in the face of the horse are [the two parts ] where his forehead meets the bone of his nose, on the right and left of the xulayoqaA=' , sloping towards the eye; and the xulayoqaA=' is [the part ] between the eyes; and some call it the xaloqaA=' . (TA.) -A2- A_in~a A^axolaqa bika A^ano tafoEala ka*aA is a phrase mentioned by Ks, as meaning Verily the most apt, meet, suitable, fit, or proper, thing for thee to do is such a thing. (TA.)

definition: (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ dubosN (M) and ↓ dibisN (K) The expressed juice of fresh ripe dates;
sourceDefinition: (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and ↓ dubosN (M) and ↓ dibisN (K) The expressed juice of fresh ripe dates; (A, Mgh, Msb;) what flows from fresh ripe dates; (S;) the honey of dates; [i. e. the sweet, thick, or inspissated, juice thereof; ] (M, K;) the expressed juice of dates, (M,) or of fresh ripe dates not cooked: (AHn, M:) what is called SaqorN in the dial. of the people of ElMedeeneh: said by some to be the honey of fresh ripe dates: by some, what flows, or exudes, from raisins and from fresh grapes: and by some, what flows from the baskets of dates: (TA:) [see also rub~N , in an explanation of which the inspissated juice of any fruit is termed its dibos :] also the honey of bees, Easalu Aln~aHolu : so in the copies of the K and in [some of the copies of] the A; a signification not known; but [AHn] EdDeenawaree mentions the word dabaAsaAtN , and explains it as signifying “ domestic bee-hives; ” and by this it is seen that the application of dbs to what bees eject may be correct: or the true reading may be Easalu Aln~axoli , with x , as in some copies of the A; and it may be meant as explaining what precedes, meaning the expressed juice of the fruit of the palm-tree, by a kind of trope; though, as such, a useless repetition: but it is said in the O, on the authority of IDrd, that bees' honey is called ↓ dibisN : (TA:) the vulgar apply the word to [the inspissated juice of fresh ripe grapes, which resembles thick honey: and sometimes to] the honey of raisins. (MF.) -A2- See also dabosN .

sourceDefinition: , applied to a horse, and to a sheep or goat, Having a black head, the rest being white: (S, Msb, * K:) or, as some say, having a black head and neck, (Msb, TA,) the rest being white: (TA:) or having a white head and neck, the rest being black: (TA:) fem. daroEaA='u : (S, Msb:) pl. duroEN : (S:) or daroEaA='u signifies having what is termed daraEN [q. v.]; applied to a sheep or goat, (K,) and to a mare: (TA:) or a sheep or goat black in the body, and white in the head: or black in the neck and head, the rest of her being white: or, accord. to AZ, a ewe having a black neck: or, accord. to Aboo-Sa'eed, sheep or goats differing in colour: or, accord. to ISh, black except in having the neck white: and red [or brown ], but having the neck white: and also, having the head with the neck white: accord. to Az, the right explanation is that given by AZ, meaning having the fore part black; being likened to the nights termed duraEN ; or the latter are likened to the former: and hence, (TA,) ― -b2- layolapN daroEaA='u (tropical:) A night of which the moon rises at the dawn, (K,) or at the commencement of the dawn; the rest thereof being black, and dark. (TA.) And ↓ layaAlK duraEN , (S, K,) said by AHát to have been heard by him only on the authority of AO, but so accord. to As and A 'Obeyd and AHeyth, (TA,) and duroEN ; (K;) the former contr. to rule, for by rule it should be duroEN , its sing. being daroEaA='u ; (A 'Obeyd, S;) or, accord. to AHeyth, you say valaAvN duraEN wavalaAvN ZulamN , and duraEN and ZulamN are pls. of ↓ duroEapN and ZulomapN , not of daroEaA='u and ZalomaA='u ; and Az says that this is correct and regular; but IB says that daroEaA='u has duraEN for its pl. for the purpose of assimilation to ZulamN in the saying valaAvN ZulamN wavalaAvN duraEN , and that no other instance had been heard by him of a word of the measure faEolaA='u having a pl. of the measure fuEalN ; (TA;) (tropical:) Three nights of the month which follow those called AlbiyDu ; (As, S, K; *) namely, the sixteenth and seventeenth and eighteenth nights; (TA;) because of the blackness of their first parts, and the whiteness of the rest thereof: (S, K:) there is no difference in what As and AZ and ISh say respecting them: but some say that they are the thirteenth and fourteenth and fifteenth; because part of them is black and part of them white: [this, however, seems to have originated from a misunderstanding of an explanation running thus; three nights of the month which follow those called AlbiyD , which, meaning the latter, are the thirteenth &c.; for the thirteenth and fourteenth and fifteenth are all white:] or, accord. to AO, All~ayaAliY Ald~uraEu signifies the nights of which the fore parts are black and the latter parts white, of the end of the month; and those of which the fore parts are white and the latter parts black, of the commencement of the month. (TA.) ― -b3- A^adoraEu also signifies (assumed tropical:) One whose father is free, or an Arab, and whose mother is a slave; syn. hajiynN ; (K;) as also muEalohajN . (TA.) And qawomN duroEN (tropical:) A people, or company of men, of whom half are white and half black. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: A certain garment, [ a tunic, ] like that called ↓ dur~aAEapN , never of anything but wool, (Lth, K,) [ and having sleeves; for] mention is made, in a trad., of a mdrEp narrow in the sleeve; wherefore the wearer, in performing the ablution termed wuDuwo' , put forth his arm from beneath the mdrEp , and so performed that ablution: (TA:) accord. to some, the ↓ dr~AEp is a [garment of the kind called ] jub~ap , slit in the fore part; (TA;) [thus resembling a kind of jub~ap worn by persons in Northern Africa, reaching to, or below, the knees, and having the two front edges sewed together from the bottom, or nearly so, to about the middle of the breast: it is said in the MA to be a wide vest or shirt; a large jub~ap : and the midoraEap is there said to be a woollen dur~aAEap ; a woollen tunic: El-Makreezee (cited by De Sacy in his “ Chrest. Arabe, ” 2nd ed., vol. i., p. 125,) describes the ↓ drA~Ep as a garment worn in Egypt particularly by Wezeers, slit in the fore part to near the head of the heart, with buttons and loops: Golius describes it as “ tunica gossipina, fere grossior; ” adding, “ estque exterior tum virilis tum muliebris; ” as on the authority of J, who says nothing of the kind, and of the Loghat Neamet-Allah: and as epomis, seu amiculum quod humeris injicitur; on the authority of Ibn-Maaroof: J only says,] the ↓ midoraE and midoraEap are one; and ↓ dur~aAEapN is sing. of, or signifies one of what are called, daraAriyEu : (S:) the pl. of mdrEp is madaAriEu . (MA.) -A2- Also The [ appendage called ] Suf~ap [q. v.] of a raHol [or camel's saddle ], when the heads of the waAsiTap [or fore part (Az says the wasaT , accord. to the TA,)] and the A=xirap [or hinder part ] appear from [ above ] it. (K.)

(M.) ― -b6- Also, the fem., accord. to A'Obeyd, Having wide bones.
